4 [[Pacific Coast Conference|PCC]] (1924, 1926–1927, 1929) | awards = [[Amos Alonzo Stagg Award]] (1948) | coaching_records = | CFBHOF_year = 1951 | CFBHOF_id = 1313 }} '''Glenn Scobey Warner''' (April 5, 1871 – September 7, 1954), most commonly known as '''Pop Warner''', was an American [[college football]] coach at various institutions who is responsible for several key aspects of the modern game. Included among his innovations are the [[Single-wing formation|single and double wing]] formations (precursors of the modern [[Spread offense|spread]] and [[shotgun formation]]s), the [[Three-point stance|three point stance]] and the body [[Blocking (American football)|blocking]] technique.{{cite web|url=http://gnb.scout.com/a.z?s=61&p=2&c=653427|title=Chalk Talk: the Single-Wing|date=June 21, 2007 |website=scout.com|author=Jeremy Stoltz|access-date=September 24, 2016}} Fellow pioneer coach [[Amos Alonzo Stagg]] called Warner "one of the excellent creators".{{Harvnb|Pope|page=293}}{{cite journal|pages=19–27|journal=Quest|title=The Myth of "Pop Warner": Carlisle Revisited|date=1978|volume=30|issue=1|author=Reet A. Howell|doi=10.1080/00336297.1978.10702797}} He was inducted as a coach into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] as part of its inaugural class in 1951. He also contributed to a junior football program which became known as [[Pop Warner Little Scholars]], a popular youth American football organization.{{cite web|website=www.popwarner.com |url=http://www.popwarner.com/About_Us.htm|access-date=February 23, 2016|title=About Us|archive-date=March 5, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305121933/http://www.popwarner.com/about_us.htm}} In the early 1900s, he created a premier football program at the [[Carlisle Indian Industrial School]]—a federally-funded, off-reservation [[Native Americans in the United States|American Indian]] boarding school.{{cite web|url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-early-history-of-footballs-forward-pass-78015237/?no-ist|title=The Early History of Football's Forward Pass|date=December 28, 2010|website=smithsonian.com|author=Jim Morrison|access-date=October 2, 2016}} He also coached teams to four [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championships]]: [[Pittsburgh Panthers football|Pittsburgh]] in [[1915 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1915]], [[1916 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1916]], and [[1918 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1918]] and [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford]] in [[1926 Stanford football team|1926]]. In all, he was head coach at the [[Georgia Bulldogs football|University of Georgia]] (1895–1896), [[Iowa State Cyclones football|Iowa Agricultural College and Model Farm]] (1895–1899), [[Cornell Big Red football|Cornell University]] (1897–1898 and 1904–1906), [[Carlisle Indians football|Carlisle]] (1899–1903 and 1907–1914), Pittsburgh (1915–1923), Stanford (1924–1932) and [[Temple Owls football|Temple University]] (1933–1938), compiling a career [[college football]] record of 319–106–32. Predating [[Bear Bryant]], [[Eddie Robinson (American football coach)|Eddie Robinson]], and [[Joe Paterno]], he once had the most wins of any coach in college football history.{{cite web|url=http://newsok.com/article/2724333|title=Father Football The Bowden family is synonymous with success|date=December 23, 2000|website=newsok.com|author=Bob Hersom|access-date=September 24, 2016}} ==Early years== Warner was born April 5, 1871, on a farm in [[Springville, New York]]. He was the son of William Warner, a [[cavalry]] officer in the [[American Civil War]], and schoolteacher Adaline Scobey.{{Harvnb|Danzig|page=224}}{{Harvnb|Miller|page=3}} In 1878 a railroad came to Springville, and four years later the family moved to a house on East Main Street. Plump as a child, Warner was sometimes known as "Butter".{{Harvnb|Miller|page=5}} He began playing [[baseball]] at an early age, and was a skilled [[pitcher]].{{Harvnb|Miller|page=6}} Nobody in town owned a [[Ball (gridiron football)|football]]; his only exposure to the new sport at a young age was with an inflated cow's bladder, and as few knew the rules, the game more resembled [[soccer]]. Warner's East Main Street house attracted a number of friends; when a neighbor told his mother that the boys' play would damage her lawn, she replied: "I'm raising boys, not grass." In 1889 at 19 years old, Warner graduated from [[Springville-Griffith Institute]] and joined his family in moving down to [[Wichita Falls, Texas]], to work on their newly purchased cattle and wheat ranch totaling over hundreds of acres.{{Harvnb|Anderson|page=21}} Aside from ranching, Warner got a job assisting a tinsmith.{{Harvnb|Anderson|page=22}} He was already interested in art as a child, learning how to [[painting|paint]] [[watercolors|watercolor]] landscapes, and as a tinsmith he learned how to use tools to make things like cups, teapots, baking pans, and lanterns.{{refn|group=n|Some consider these skills and experiences those that first inspired Warner to later make improvements to shoulder and thigh pads, as well as tackling dummies.}} ===Student years at Cornell=== In 1892, Warner returned to Springville and began to use his cowboy experience to [[gambling|gamble]] on [[horse races]].{{Harvnb|Anderson|page=23}} Although he had no interest in college, soon after coming back he attended [[Cornell Law School]], as he had lost all of his money at the races.{{Harvnb|Anderson|page=24}} Later Warner wrote "I dare not write to my father and tell him I was broke"—he felt that the only way to get funds was to inform his father that he had decided to study law. His father, who had always wanted him to be a lawyer, sent him {{US$|100|1892|round=-2|about=yes|long=no}}.{{Harvnb|Miller|page=9}}{{Inflation-fn|US}} Eventually, Warner became known as "Pop" because he was one of the oldest students at [[Cornell University|Cornell]].{{Harvnb|Pope|page=291}} Warner graduated from Cornell in 1894 and began working as an attorney in [[Buffalo, New York]].{{cite web|url=http://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/sports-outdoor-recreation/glenn-pop-warner-1871-1954|title=Glenn "Pop" Warner (1871–1954)|website=New Georgia Encyclopedia|access-date=December 23, 2015}} This job only lasted for a few months.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=11}} ====Playing career==== On Warner's train ride to [[Ithaca, New York|Ithaca]], where Cornell is located, he met [[Carl Johanson]], then [[Cornell Big Red football|Cornell's football]] coach, who was impressed by Warner's weight (200 pounds).{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=4}} Johanson practically ordered Warner to attend practice. This happened even though Warner admitted that he had never handled a real football.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=4}} Despite his commitment to football, at the time Warner's true passion was baseball. During one of his first practices at Cornell he badly injured his shoulder and never played serious baseball again.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=5}} Warner also participated in [[track and field]] and was the school's [[heavyweight]] [[boxing]] champion for two years.{{Harvnb|Pope|page=295}} =====Football===== [[File:Pop Warner, c. 1894, in Cornell uniform.jpg|thumb|upright=0.65|Warner in a Cornell uniform, c. 1894|alt=Large young man in a turtleneck and football pants, with hands on hips]] During his three years at Cornell, Warner played as a [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] on the football team. Even though he graduated in the spring of 1894, he returned as a post-graduate and was named [[Captain (sports)|captain]] of the [[1894 Cornell Big Red football team|1894 team]], which had a 6–4–1 record.{{cite web|title=1894 Cornell Big Red Schedule and Results |publisher=Sports Reference |work=SR/College Football |access-date=December 10, 2015 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/cornell/1894-schedule.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222120939/http://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/cornell/1894-schedule.html |archive-date=December 22, 2015 }}{{refn|group="n"|That year Cornell lost to [[1894 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan]], marking the first time Michigan was able to beat an [[Ivy League]] team.{{cite news|title=The Michiganders Won: A {{Sic|?|hide=y|Hotly|-}}Contested Game of Football from Cornell—Score 12 to 4|newspaper=The Daily Republican (Decatur, Il)|date=November 26, 1894}}}} Due to the then-tradition of alumni coming back to assist their undergraduate teams in [[College rivalry|rivalry]] games, Cornell's coach [[Marshall Newell]] left for several weeks to assist [[1894 Harvard Crimson football team|Harvard]] in its [[Harvard–Yale football rivalry|rivalry game]] with [[1894 Yale Bulldogs football team|Yale]].{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=10}} As a captain, Warner was put in charge during the coach's absence.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=10}} It was during this time that Warner came up with his first original [[American football plays|play]]: Three [[running back|back]]s who normally protected the [[Rush (gridiron football)|rusher]] would fake a run to one side, while the [[quarterback]] kept the ball and would [[hand-off|hand]] it to the runner, who now had an open field to run through on the other side.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=10}} During the first in-game execution of the play, Warner [[Carry (gridiron football)|carried]] the ball and was able to run clear for 25 yards. However, as Warner was a guard and not a runner, he was incorrectly holding the ball, and [[fumble]]d upon being [[Tackle (football move)|tackled]].{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=10}} ==Coaching career== === Iowa State, Georgia and Cornell === In the spring of 1895, Warner was asked for a reference to fill the vacant head coaching position at [[Iowa State University|Iowa Agricultural College]], in [[Ames, Iowa]].{{refn|group="n"|In 1895, the university was known as the Iowa Agricultural College and Model Farm.}} Instead of giving a reference, Warner himself applied for the job and received an offer for $25 per week ({{Inflation|US|25|1895|r=-1|fmt=eq}}).{{Inflation-fn|US}} At the same time, he decided to apply to other schools and received an offer of $34 per week ({{Inflation|US|34|1895|r=-1|fmt=eq}}) from the [[University of Georgia]] in [[Athens, Georgia]].{{Harvnb|Reed|date=1949|pages=3441–3445}}{{refn|group="n"|For a ten-week season ($340), {{Inflation|US|340|1895|r=-2|fmt=eq}}.{{Inflation-fn|US}} For the 1895–96 academic year, Georgia's entire student body consisted of 126 students.{{Harvnb|Reed|date=1949|page=1696 }}}} Because Iowa State began its season in August—almost one and a half months prior to the beginning in Georgia—Warner was able to work out a deal. For {{US$|150|1895|round=-2|about=yes|long=no}},{{Inflation-fn|US}} he would coach in Iowa from August until the second week of September, and then head to Georgia and begin coaching there.{{Harvnb|Anderson|page=31}} ====Iowa State==== Ultimately, not only did Warner end up coaching at Iowa State before his time at Georgia; but while in Athens, he also received weekly updates from Iowa and sent back telegraphs with detailed advice for the following week.{{Harvnb|Anderson|page=35}} One story recounts that in the middle of September (just before leaving for Georgia), Warner took his team north west for a previously agreed-upon game against the Butte Athletic Club of [[Butte, Montana]].{{Harvnb|Anderson|page=32}} Apparently overconfident, Warner bet the entire sum of his Iowa State wages—{{US$|150|1895|round=-2|about=yes|long=no}}{{Inflation-fn|US}}—on his team's victory.{{Harvnb|Anderson|page=34}} At halftime, his team trailed 10–2. Warner decided to enter the game, filling in at the guard position. Though this had a positive impact, it was not sufficient as his team still lost 12–10. In a 1947 publication by Francis J. Powers, there is an alternate take on the causes of the Butte loss: "The game was played on a field as devoid of grass as a glacier and there was nothing green ... It was impossible for the center to snap the ball to the quarterback on the bounce or even roll it without chances for a fumble ... Whenever Iowa State threatened to score, the referee (a home towner) would make a decision which chilled the Cyclones' offense ... spectators, who followed up and down the sidelines, would whip out their six shooters and blaze away with enthusiasm, which also chilled the Iowa college boys."{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=15, 16}} In order to try and make up for losing all of his Iowa State wages, Warner worked out a deal where, for {{US$|30|1895|round=-2|about=yes|long=no}},{{Inflation-fn|US}} he would stay in contact with Iowa State while at Georgia. Soon after Warner left for Georgia, Iowa State had its first official college game of the season. In [[Evanston, Illinois|Evanston]], just north of Chicago, [[Underdog (term)|underdog]] Iowa State defeated [[1895 Northwestern Purple football team|Northwestern]] 36–0. A ''Chicago Tribune'' headline read, "Struck by a [[Tornado|Cyclone]]".{{Cite news|title=Struck by a Cyclone|date=September 29, 1895|work=Chicago Tribune |url=http://archives.chicagotribune.com/1895/09/29/page/6/article/struck-by-a-cyclone}} Since then, Iowa State teams have been known as the [[Iowa State Cyclones|Cyclones]].{{Cite web |title=Historic Athletic Team Names – Cyclones definitely included!|date=February 7, 2011|website=Cardinal Tales: The Blog of Special Collections and University Archives at Iowa State University |url=https://isuspecialcollections.wordpress.com/2011/02/07/historic-athletic-team-names-cyclones-definitely-included/|access-date=November 9, 2016|archive-date=September 12, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150912184605/https://isuspecialcollections.wordpress.com/2011/02/07/historic-athletic-team-names-cyclones-definitely-included/}} The team finished with three wins and three losses and, like Georgia, retained Warner for the following season. In 1896, Iowa State had eight wins and two losses.{{Harvnb|Iowa State University|page=138}} Despite leaving Georgia for Cornell in 1897, Warner remained head coach at Iowa State for another three years, posting winning records. ====Georgia==== [[File:WarnerinAthens.jpg|alt=Man in a coat and hat faces left|thumb|Warner on the Georgia sidelines]] In Warner's [[1895 Georgia Bulldogs football team|first season at Georgia]], he was hired at a salary of $34 per week. The school was a [[Charter#Colloquial uses|charter member]] of the [[Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Association]] (SIAA), the first athletic conference in the [[Southern United States|South]].{{Harvnb|Roza|pages=1–3}} The football team had three wins and four losses, including a [[1895 Georgia vs. North Carolina football game|loss to North Carolina]] from a not-yet-legal [[forward pass]].{{refn|[[1895 North Carolina Tar Heels football team|North Carolina]] was "in a punting situation and a Georgia rush seemed destined to block the ball. The punter ([[Joel Whitaker]], out of desperation) with an impromptu dash to his right, tossed the ball and it was caught by [[George Stephens (American football)|George Stephens]], who ran 70 yards for a touchdown." Warner complained to the referee that the play was illegal. However, the referee let the play stand because he did not see the pass.{{cite web |url=http://www.tarheeltimes.com/2006/08/tar_heels_credi.html |title=Tar Heels Credited with Throwing First Forward Pass |access-date=July 12, 2011| work=Tar Heel Times| publisher=tarheeltimes.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061219050634/http://www.tarheeltimes.com/2006/08/tar_heels_credi.html |archive-date=December 19, 2006}} The teams played a second time and North Carolina won 10–6.|group="n"}} He was rehired at a salary of $40 per week,{{refn|group=n|"I thought more of that contract than any I have ever received for coaching a football team" said Warner.{{Harvnb|Woodruff|1928a|page=38}}}} and the [[1896 Georgia Bulldogs football team|next season]] Georgia had one of the school's first great teams.{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/1944523//|title=Brown Calls Vanderbilt '06 Best Eleven South Ever Had|date=February 19, 1911|work=Atlanta Constitution|page=52|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=March 8, 2015}} {{Open access}}{{Harvnb|Garbin|pages=4–8}} With an undefeated record, the team won its first conference title.{{Harvnb|Miller|pages=24, 26}}{{cite web|url=http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/conference_champs/champions.php?conid=181|title=Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Association: Conference Championships|website=cfbdatawarehouse.com|access-date=April 5, 2008|archive-date=September 30, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930014352/http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/conference_champs/champions.php?conid=181|url-status=dead}} It also avenged the loss to North Carolina, winning 24–16, "For the first time in Southern football history the football supremacy of Virginia and North Carolina was successfully challenged."{{Harvnb|Woodruff|1928a|page=53}} During those two years Warner also played two games against [[John Heisman]], another future coaching legend. Heisman was the head coach at [[Auburn University]], and they faced each other in the [[1895 Georgia Bulldogs football team|1895]] and [[1896 Georgia Bulldogs football team|1896]] games of the "[[Deep South's Oldest Rivalry]]," an annual confrontation which has continued to the present day. In 1895, the [[1895 Auburn Tigers football team|Auburn Tigers]] defeated the Bulldogs 12–6. The Auburn team was led by [[quarterback]] [[Reynolds Tichenor|Reynolds "Tick" Tichenor]], known for his [[punt returns]].{{Harvnb|Stegeman|pages=85–91}} Tichenor had executed the first "[[Hidden ball trick|hidden-ball trick"]] in an earlier Auburn game against [[1895 Vanderbilt Commodores football team|Vanderbilt]],{{refn|Auburn still lost to Vanderbilt 9–6, the first game in the south decided by a [[field goal]].{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=897&dat=19310124&id=-aNaAAAAIBAJ&pg=4042,1045626|author=Alan Gould|title=Sport Slants|work=Prescott Evening Courier|date=January 24, 1931}}|group="n"}} and used it again against Georgia.{{Harvnb|Cook|page=27}} The next year, Tichenor faced Georgia's [[Richard Von Albade Gammon]], a star quarterback in his first year under Warner. Both quarterbacks played well and, unlike the previous year, Warner's team won 16–6.{{refn|Richard Gammon died soon after the following season's game against the [[1897 Virginia Cavaliers football team|University of Virginia]]. Tichenor and Gammon played together in 1897 as Tichenor transferred to Georgia, taking Gammon's place as the starting quarterback, who shifted to fullback. In the game against Virginia, Gammon was playing defense and suffered a severe concussion after taking part in a tackle. With coaches' help Gammon was able to walk, but he lost his consciousness shortly after getting off the field. He remained unconscious and died early the next morning.{{Harvnb|Edwards|page=244}}|group="n"}} The second touchdown came right after the first [[onside kick]] in the South.{{Harvnb|Woodruff|1928a|page=68}} ==== Cornell ==== After Georgia's outstanding 1896 performance, Warner returned to his ''[[alma mater]]'' Cornell at twice his Georgia salary.{{Harvnb|Miller|page=27}} While remaining head coach at [[Iowa State]], he coached Cornell to records of 5–3–1 in [[1897 Cornell Big Red football team|1897]] and 10–2 in [[1898 Cornell Big Red football team|1898]];{{cite web|url=http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/coaching/alltime_coach_year_by_year.php?coachid=2440|title=Glenn Scobey "Pop" Warner Records by Year|website=cfbdatawarehouse.com|access-date=September 29, 2016|archive-date=September 19, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100919220633/http://cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/coaching/alltime_coach_year_by_year.php?coachid=2440|url-status=dead}} in the latter season, Cornell outscored its opponents 296–29.{{Harvnb|Miller|page=33, 34}} Despite its 1898 success, tension existed within the team, as its assistant coach (backed by a large proportion of the players) lobbied to replace Warner. Acknowledging an issue with his leadership, Warner resigned. =====Return to Cornell===== In 1904, after five years at Carlisle (see below), Warner returned to Cornell but his [[1904 Cornell Big Red football team|1904 team]] featuring Clemson transfer [[James Lynah]] was little improved over the [[1903 Cornell Big Red football team|previous year]]. The following two years were better, with the [[1905 Cornell Big Red football team|1905 team]] losing to undefeated champion [[1905 Penn Quakers football team|Penn]] by one point. Their game [[1906 Cornell Big Red football team|next year]] was a scoreless tie, and Cornell lost only one game that season (to [[1906 Princeton Tigers football team|Princeton]]).{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=26}} === Carlisle === After leaving Cornell the first time, Warner became head coach of the [[Carlisle Indians football|football team]] at [[Carlisle Indian Industrial School]] the first Native American boarding school.{{cite web|url=http://home.epix.net/~landis/histry.html|title=Carlisle Indian Industrial School History|access-date=October 29, 2016}} Its late-nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century football teams were nationally prominent,{{Harvnb|National Collegiate Athletic Association|2007|page=398}} and Warner was paid {{US$|1200|1899|round=-3|about=yes|long=no}},{{Inflation-fn|US}} an exceptionally high salary for a coach at the time. His previous Cornell team had once faced Carlisle, and he had been impressed by his opponent's approach to the game. Since the players were outweighed by every other team in the nation, they relied on speed and agility instead of size and physical force. Despite those strengths, Cornell won the game 23 to 6. The referee was a former Cornell graduate and was accused of helping out Cornell during the game. After the match, while addressing the journalists, Warner acknowledged that there had been assistance from the referee. He stated that "We outscored 'em but we didn't defeat 'em, if you follow me."{{Harvnb|Anderson|page=37}} It has been said that after that game he considered Carlisle to be the future of college football.{{Harvnb|Miller|page=31}} The head coach dealt with young players who differed from the white, East-Coast students with whom he had previously worked. At the beginning, he used the then-customary coaching methods of rough language and a strict routine.{{Harvnb|Pope|page=294}} The Native American students were unaccustomed to such an approach, and several key players stopped attending practices. Warner adjusted his technique, saying that he "found I could get better results. I don't think I ever swore at a player from that time. Maybe I did a little cussing, now and then, but never at players."{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=18}} His coaching brought immediate improvement. In [[1897 Carlisle Indians football team|1897]] and [[1898 Carlisle Indians football team|1898]], the Carlisle teams had 6–4 records. In [[1899 Carlisle Indians football team|1899]] (Warner's first year), Carlisle won nine and lost two games—to the country's two best teams: [[1899 Harvard Crimson football team|Harvard]] and [[1899 Princeton Tigers football team|Princeton]]. That year saw Carlisle's first major victory, against one of the "[[Big Three (colleges)|Big Four]]" teams,{{refn|group="n"|The original term was the Big Three – the dominant programs of Harvard, Yale and Princeton. By the beginning of the century Penn also became considered one of the elite football schools.{{cite journal|journal=College Football Historical Society Newsletter|volume=17|url=http://library.la84.org/SportsLibrary/CFHSN/CFHSNv17/CFHSNv17n1d.pdf|author=Tom Benjey|pages=7–10|title=Carlisle vs. Big Four|via=[[LA84]]}}}} beating [[1899 Penn Quakers football team|Penn]] 16–5.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=18}} At the end of the season, the school played [[1899 Columbia Lions football team|Columbia]] at the [[Polo Grounds]] in New York City, a premier sports venue at the time, defeating them 42–0.{{refn|group="n"|Columbia had also previously [[Upset (sports)|upset]] one of the Big Four – having beaten Yale 5–0.{{cite web |title=1899 Columbia Lions Schedule and Results|publisher=Sports-Reference |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/columbia/1899-schedule.html |date=January 18, 2016 |access-date=January 18, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160118234334/http://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/columbia/1899-schedule.html |archive-date=January 18, 2016 }}}} The Columbia game was the first time that a crouching start, a form of what is now known as a [[Three-point stance|three point stance]], was used by the [[running back]]s. Before Warner's innovation, the stance for a back before the ball was snapped was bent forward with his feet well apart and his hands on his knees. Warner realized that if his players took a stance similar to the one taken by [[sprint (running)|sprinters]], the legs would be bent, the back leaning forward, with one hand on the ground and the other arm cocked back to the thigh/hip region. Like with sprinters, this similar stance maximized the speed of his players. Shortly after, it became the standard football stance for both backs and [[Lineman (American football)|linemen]].{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=19}} [[File:1903carlisle.jpg|thumb|upright=1.35|alt=A football team picture, with men in sweaters|[[1903 Carlisle Indians football team|1903 Carlisle Indians]], with Warner at top right]] At the end of 1899, Warner was appointed the school's athletic director and his salary more than doubled.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=21}} A track-and-field program was started that year. Warner knew little about the sport; to prepare as coach he bought every book available and consulted [[John Francis Moakley|Jack Moakley]] and [[Mike Murphy (trainer and coach)|Mike Murphy]], two of the era's leading head coaches.{{cite web |url=http://www.usatf.org/HallOfFame/TF/showBio.asp?HOFIDs=111|title=John (Jack) Moakley|publisher=[[National Track & Field Hall of Fame]]|access-date=October 2, 2016}}{{Cite news|title=Murphy Is Crowned The Wizard Trainer of the Civilized World|date=August 9, 1908|newspaper=Butte Miner}} The program was successful; running was a Native American tradition, and students from the [[Southwestern United States|Southwest]] were known for their stamina in long-distance races.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=21}}{{cite web|url=http://library.nau.edu/speccoll/exhibits/hopitg/Hopilesson4.html|title=Lesson Plan Four: Hopi Running|website=library.nau.edu|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160130020754/http://library.nau.edu/speccoll/exhibits/hopitg/Hopilesson4.html|archive-date=January 30, 2016|access-date=July 1, 2016}} Warner's next two years were less fruitful. The [[1900 Carlisle Indians football team|1900 football team]] went 6–4–1, losing three games to the Big Four, and the [[1901 Carlisle Indians football team|1901 season]] was a losing one, with Carlisle posting a 5–7–1 record. The [[1902 Carlisle Indians football team|following year]], the team posted an improved 8–3 record,{{cite web|title=1902 Carlisle Indians Roster {{!}} College Football at Sports-Reference.com |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/carlisle/1902-roster.html |date=January 19, 2016|access-date=January 19, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160119192404/http://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/carlisle/1902-roster.html |archive-date=January 19, 2016 }} when Warner began implementing [[double pass|double (lateral) passes]]. Carlisle's quarterback [[Jimmy Johnson (quarterback)|Jimmy Johnson]] would make a lateral pass to the halfback running towards the sideline, bringing the defense with him as he tossed the ball back to the fast-running Johnson. In 1902, Warner played one professional football game for the [[Syracuse Athletic Club]] during the [[World Series of Football (1902)|first World Series of Football]] at [[Madison Square Garden (1890)|Madison Square Garden]]. In the first professional [[indoor American football|indoor football game]], Syracuse defeated the heavily favored [[New York (World Series of Football)|New York]] team. During the series, Warner was seriously cut on the side of his head. Although he laughed it off at first, the injury turned out to be more serious and he was replaced with [[Blondy Wallace]] for the rest of the series.{{cite magazine |title=The First Football World Series| journal=Coffin Corner |volume=2 |issue=Annual |year=1980 |pages=1–8 |url=http://www.profootballresearchers.org/coffin-corner80s/02-An-054.pdf |author=Carroll, Bob}} For the tournament, Warner and the other team members each earned {{US$|23|1902|round=-1|about=yes|long=no}}, although each player's expected share had been {{US$|300|1902|round=-3|about=yes|long=no}}; it was a financial failure.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=23}}{{Inflation-fn|US}} Carlisle's [[1903 Carlisle Indians football team|1903 season]] was a success, with only two losses. The 12–11 defeat by [[1913 Harvard Crimson football team|Harvard]] is known for the "hunch-back", or "[[hidden ball trick|hidden-ball]]", play which Warner learned from Heisman;{{Harvnb|Woodruff|1928a|page=40}} he had a tailor sew elastic bands into the waists of several players' jerseys before the game so the play could be executed. It was used during a Harvard [[Kickoff (American football)|kickoff]]; when the ball was caught, Carlisle formed a circle around the [[kick return|returner]] and pushed the ball up the back of the player's (altered) [[Jersey (clothing)|jersey]]. Carlisle then broke the [[huddle]] and spread out in different directions. Each player except the returner (who had the hidden ball) pretended to carry the football. The ruse confused the Harvard players, who scrambled to find the ball carrier, and the returner (ignored, with both hands free) ran untouched into the [[end zone]].{{cite web |url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=10217979|title=Gridiron Guts: The Story of Football's Carlisle Indians|website=NPR|date= May 19, 2007|access-date=September 24, 2016}}{{cite magazine |url=http://www.newsweek.com/id/35160|title=Football, the Indian Way|magazine=Newsweek|date=April 27, 2007|access-date=September 24, 2016}} Warner's next step was a brief return to Cornell.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=26}} ==== Back to Carlisle ==== After three years at Cornell, Warner returned to Carlisle.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=26}} He considered his second stint there his best.{{refn|group="n"|Warner was once asked by a reporter from the ''Carlisle Herald'' to name an all-time Carlisle football team. It included in the line: Albert Exendine, [[Martin Wheelock]], [[Bemus Pierce]], William Garlowe, Charles Dillon, Emil Hauser, [[Eddie Rogers|Edward Rogers]]; and in the backfield: Jimmy Johnson, Jim Thorpe, [[Joe Guyon]], and Pete Hauser.{{cite news|url=http://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn83045433/1913-11-10/ed-1/seq-8/|work=The Washington Herald|page=8|date=November 10, 1913|title=G. U. Chances To Win Slim|author=William Peet|via=[[Chronicling America]]|access-date=April 4, 2015}} {{Open access}}}} From [[1907 Carlisle Indians football team|1907]] to [[1914 Carlisle Indians football team|1914]], the team won ten or more games a season five times. [[File:Single wing formation vs5 diagram.gif|thumb|alt=Blue and yellow figures drawn in formation|A single wing formation illustrated.]] During this time at Carlisle, Warner made several significant contributions to football offense, including the [[Blocking (American football)|body block]] technique and the [[Single-wing formation|single-]] and [[double wing formation|double]]-[[wingback (American football)|wingback]] [[Formation (American football)|formations]].{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=30, 34}} Under Warner, Carlisle quarterback [[Frank Mount Pleasant]] and [[Fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] [[Peter Hauser (American football)|Pete Hauser]] became two of the first regular [[Spiral (football)|spiral]] passers in football (the forward pass was legalized in 1906).{{cite web|url=http://www.radiolab.org/story/photos-carlisle-football/|title=Photos: Carlisle Football|website=radiolab|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160429190339/http://www.radiolab.org/story/photos-carlisle-football/|archive-date=April 29, 2016|access-date=January 21, 2016}}{{cite journal|journal=College Football Historical Society Newsletter|volume=18|url=http://library.la84.org/SportsLibrary/CFHSN/CFHSNv18/CFHSNv18n4c.pdf|author=Tom Benjey|pages=4–8|title=Beginnings of Modern Football|via=[[LA84]]}}{{refn|group="n"|Warner credited Hauser with tossing the first one.{{Harvnb|King|page=142}}}} In [[1908 Carlisle Indians football team|1908]] he introduced the technique of body [[Blocking (American football)|blocking]], instead of blocking with the shoulders.{{Harvnb|Otto|page=202}} Warner considered the 1907 Carlisle team "about as perfect a football machine as I ever sent on the field".{{cite web|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2007/more/04/19/carlisle0423/index.html|title=The Team that Invented Football|website=www.nativevillage.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160508010811/http://nativevillage.org/Messages%20from%20the%20People/team_that_invented_football.htm|archive-date=May 8, 2016|access-date=March 23, 2016|author=Sally Jenkins. Sports Illustrated.}}{{refn|group="n"|Quarterback Mount Pleasant was also on the 1904 and 1908 U.S. Olympic track and field teams, and at end was future member of the College Football Hall of Fame and future coach [[Albert Exendine]].}} The team posted a 10–1 record, outscored opponents 267–62 and pioneered an elegant, high-speed passing game; it was one of the first teams to regularly throw the ball deep downfield. For the first time in 11 years, Carlisle defeated [[1907 Harvard Crimson football team|Harvard]] on the road 23–15.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=30, 34}} Carlisle also won 26–6 over [[1907 Penn Quakers football team|Penn]].{{cite journal|url=http://library.la84.org/SportsLibrary/CFHSN/CFHSNv17/CFHSNv17n1d.pdf|journal=College Football Historical Society Newsletter|author=Tom Benjey|volume=17|page=7|title=Carlisle vs. The Big Four}} In the second play of the Penn game, Hauser threw a 40-yard spiral pass, hitting his [[Reception (gridiron football)|receiver]] in stride. At the time such a pass was stunning and unexpected, and is considered by one journalist to be an evolutionary step in the game. The 1907 season is known for Warner's first use of the single-wing formation, characterized by [[lateral pass|laterals]], [[trap run|trap]] and [[counter run|counter]] runs, and passing.{{Harvnb|Long|2015|page=104}} According to [[Sally Jenkins]], in her ''Sports Illustrated'' article on Carlisle:
To take advantage of the Indians' versatility Warner drew up a new offense ..."the Carlisle formation," but later it would be known as the single wing. It was predicated on one small move: Warner shifted a halfback out wide, to outflank the opposing [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|tackle]], forming something that looked like a wing. It opened up a world of possibilities. The Indians could line up as if to [[Punt (gridiron football)|punt]] – and then throw. No one would know whether they were going to run, pass or kick. For added measure Warner taught his quarterbacks to sprint out a few yards to their left or their right, buying more time to throw. The rest of the players flooded downfield and knocked down any opponent who might be able to [[Interception#American/Canadian football|intercept]] or bat away the pass.
[[File:1911 Carlisle Indians FB team.jpg|thumb|upright=1.35|alt=Team picture of men in sweaters|The 1911 Carlisle Indians pose with a game ball from their upset of Harvard]] The 1907 team included a young [[Jim Thorpe]], considered one of the greatest athletes who ever lived.{{Cite news | url=https://www.teamusa.org/News/2012/June/11/Jim-Thorpe-The-Greatest-Athlete-A-Century-Later-June-11-2012.aspx | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120612190100/http://www.teamusa.org/News/2012/June/11/Jim-Thorpe-The-Greatest-Athlete-A-Century-Later-June-11-2012.aspx | url-status=dead | archive-date=June 12, 2012 | title=Jim Thorpe: 'The Greatest Athlete' A Century Later | first=Doug | last=Williams | date=June 11, 2012 | work=Team USA | access-date=October 28, 2016}}{{cite web|url=http://www.notablebiographies.com/St-Tr/Thorpe-Jim.html|title=Jim Thorpe Biography – life, children, name, death, history, school, mother, young, son|website=Notable Biographies|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160220064827/http://www.notablebiographies.com/St-Tr/Thorpe-Jim.html|archive-date=February 20, 2016|access-date=January 21, 2016}} Thorpe weighed just {{Convert|155|lb|kg|abbr=on}}, light for a football player. Warner played him as a [[Substitution (sport)|substitute]], encouraging him to put his time into track and field.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=30, 34}} By 1909, Warner had Thorpe competing in track and field and he won 14 events. In 1911, Thorpe began training for the upcoming [[Summer Olympic Games|Olympics]], and won [[gold medal]]s in the [[pentathlon]] and [[decathlon]] at the [[1912 Summer Olympics|1912 Olympic Games]] in [[Stockholm]]. Thorpe’s Olympic victories in the pentathlon and decathlon at the 1912 Stockholm Games brought international attention to both Carlisle and Native American athletes; however, a year later the International Olympic Committee stripped him of his medals after it was revealed he had played semiprofessional baseball before the Games, violating the strict amateurism rules of the time, and only restored him as the sole champion in both events on the 110th anniversary of his victories in 2022.{{cite web |title=World Athletics Council restores Jim Thorpe as sole winner of 1912 Olympic decathlon and pentathlon |url=https://worldathletics.org/heritage/news/jim-thorpe-sole-decathlon-pentathlon-winner-1912-olympics |website=World Athletics |publisher=World Athletics |date=15 July 2022 |access-date=17 February 2026}}{{refn|group="n"|[[Lewis Tewanima]], another Carlisle track and field athlete who competed in Stockholm where he won the silver medal in the 10,000 meter run, was considered a ward of the state with Thorpe. Warner was delegated to accompany them to the Olympics.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=30, 34}} Warner's 1907 quarterback [[Frank Mount Pleasant]] was also an Olympic athlete who competed in the [[1908 Summer Olympics]] in [[London]].{{cite web |title=Frank Mount Pleasant Bio, Stats, and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/athletes/mo/frank-mount-pleasant-1.html |website=Olympics at Sports-Reference.com |access-date=January 21, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160205035620/http://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/athletes/mo/frank-mount-pleasant-1.html |archive-date=February 5, 2016}}}} [[File:Glenn Warner, Jim Thorpe tackling a dummy.jpg|thumb|left|alt=A man pulling a wire above his head, and another smaller man crashing into what hangs from the wire|Jim Thorpe tackling a weighted dummy on a pulley with Warner supervising, 1912.]] Carlisle football had another standout year in [[1911 Carlisle Indians football team|1911]], posting an 11–1 record. Thorpe had grown to {{Convert|180|lb|kg|abbr=on}}, big enough to be a starter. The team defeated [[1911 Harvard Crimson football team|Harvard]] 18–15, with Thorpe scoring all of Carlisle's field goals.{{Cite web |last=Richmond |first=Sam |date=November 11, 2015 |title=Jim Thorpe leads Carlisle to upset of Harvard in 1911 |url=https://www.ncaa.com/news/football/article/2015-11-11/jim-thorpe-leads-carlisle-upset-harvard-1911 |access-date=October 3, 2016 |website=ncaa.com}} [[Walter Camp]] selected Thorpe as a first-team All-American. According to one source, Thorpe was "recognized as the greatest player of the year and a man whose kicking is likely to revolutionize the game".{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/2122372//|title=The Year In Football|page=17|date=December 31, 1911|access-date=April 2, 2015|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|work=The Houston Post}} {{Open access}} Warner considered the 1912 team brilliant and adaptive, and experimented with new plays and formations. In its game against Army, Warner's team introduced a wrinkle to the wing-back system. According to Francis J. Powers, author of a book that concentrated on Warner's approach to football: [[File:Double Wing Formation.png|thumb|The double wing formation.]]
Warner had both halfbacks close to the line and flanking the defensive tackles. That was the start of the double wingback offense, which enjoyed tremendous popularity until the [[T formation]] was modernized with the man in [[Motion (gridiron football)|motion]]. The double wing became the most effective of all systems for effective forward passing since it permitted the quick release of four receivers down the field.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=30, 34}}
Carlisle dominated the next two years, with the [[1912 Carlisle Indians football team|1912]] and [[1913 Carlisle Indians football team|1913]] teams losing only one game each. Warner's salary increased to $4,500 per season ({{Inflation|US|4500|1912|r=-3|fmt=eq}}).{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=35}}{{Inflation-fn|US}} In 1914 there was an administrative change in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington]], with federal money considered better spent in the [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]] than on schools like Carlisle.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=30, 34}} Many students left, and this affected the team (which had a 5–10–1 record). After that season, Warner left Carlisle to become head coach at Pittsburgh.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=30, 34}} === Pittsburgh === [[File:PopandPeck1918Owl.jpg|thumb|upright=0.80|alt=A coach conversing with a football player|Warner and Pitt captain [[Bob Peck (football)|Bob Peck]] during the 1916 season.]] When Warner arrived at the [[University of Pittsburgh]] in [[1915 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1915]], the 128-year-old school was on a new campus with 3,900 students.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=35}} He inherited a team in good shape, full of future All-Americans,{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=35}} and coached the [[Pittsburgh Panthers football|Pittsburgh Panthers]] to their first undefeated season. Six of their eight games (all [[shutout]]s) were played at home on [[Forbes Field]], including a 45–0 victory over [[1915 Carlisle Indians football team|Carlisle]]. Warner coached his Pitt teams to 29 straight victories, and is credited with three [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championships]] (1915, 1916 and 1918).{{Harvnb|National Collegiate Athletic Association|2009|pages=76–81}} Coaching Pittsburgh from 1915 to 1923, he compiled a 60–12–4 record.{{Harvnb|University of Pittsburgh|page=150}} Although the 1915 season was a success, [[1916 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|the next year's team]] was one of the greatest of Warner's career.{{Harvnb|Danzig|page=219}} The Panthers were again undefeated and, like the previous year, six of the eight games were shutouts. Thirty-two of their 35 players were from [[Western Pennsylvania]], near Pittsburgh.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=39}} The team scored 255 points, conceding 25. Warner considered the team an improvement because its defense was more dominant than the previous year's.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=39}} The Panthers were the consensus national champions, and Warner became recognized as one of football's greatest coaches.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=41}} [[File:PopatPitt1919Owl.jpg|thumb|upright|left|alt=A smiling old man in glasses and overalls, hands on hips|Warner during the 1917 season at Pittsburgh]] In 1917 the United States entered [[World War I]], and some players (including [[Andy Hastings]] and [[James DeHart|Jimmy Dehart]]) entered military service.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=41}} Pittsburgh played an undefeated [[1917 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|full season]] despite the war, although it was not awarded the national championship.{{refn|group="n"|The team was known as "The Fighting Dentists" because on occasion every position was filled by dental students.{{Cite news|title=50th Anniversary: Last Unbeaten Pitt Team, 1917 'Fighting Dentists', Will Be Honored Saturday |work=[[Pittsburgh Tribune-Review|Daily Courier]] |date=November 2, 1967}}}} Although the team lacked the previous year's punch, it dominated the opposition. A key aspect of its success was the opposing coaches' inability to address Warner's evolving strategies; according to Powers, "His [[Reverse (American football)|reverse]] plays were a mystery, although Pop always was willing to explain them in detail to any other coach".{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=41}} Faculties had to step in to stop a decisive, postseason national championship game with John Heisman's undefeated [[1917 Georgia Tech Golden Tornado football team|Georgia Tech]] team.{{Harvnb|Woodruff|1928b|page=68}} The game was postponed until the following season, giving Tech the 1917 national championship (the first for any [[Southern United States|Southern]] school).{{cite web|url=http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/national_championships/yearly_results.php?year=1917|title=1917 National Championships|access-date=September 24, 2016|website=cfbdatawarehouse.com|archive-date=March 3, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303165330/http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/national_championships/yearly_results.php?year=1917|url-status=dead}} On November 23, 1918, the two teams played at Pittsburgh.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=42}} At the stadium the locker rooms were next to each other, with only a thin wall separating the two teams prior to the game. Heisman was first to begin an inspirational speech and it was said that he passionately described both heroes of [[Ancient Greece]] as well as the tragedy of a soldier found in his armor among the ruins of [[Pompeii]]. Because of Georgia Tech's players' silence the speech was crystal clear on the other side of the wall. Upon its finish Warner smiled and quietly told his players "Okay, boys. There's the speech. Now go out and knock them off." Pittsburgh defeated Georgia Tech 32–0.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=42}} [[File:DaviesPittGT1918.jpg|thumb|alt=A player with a football runs past others.|Tom Davies runs vs. Georgia Tech, 1918.]] The [[1918 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1918 season]] was cut short at the end of November due to the continuing effects of World War I and the [[1918 flu pandemic|influenza pandemic]].{{cite web |title=War Conditions Coupled With Epidemic Have Big Effect On 1918 Sports |date=February 3, 2016 |url=http://quod.lib.umich.edu/f/flu/5150flu.0005.515/1 |access-date=February 3, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160203014916/http://quod.lib.umich.edu/f/flu/5150flu.0005.515/1 |archive-date=February 3, 2016}} Only five games were played, and the season's final game was in Cleveland against the Naval Reserve. Warner's first loss at Pitt, it was one of the most controversial games in school history.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=50}} According to Warner and several reporters covering the game, Pitt was robbed by the [[Official (American football)|officials]].{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=50}} The referees said that the timekeeper's watch was broken, ended the first half before Pitt was able to score and allowed the Reserves extra time in the fourth quarter to pull ahead, 10–9.{{sfn|Bynum|Sciullo Jr.|Eldridge Jr.|1994|page=33}}{{sfn|Sciullo|2008|page=36}} Although he refused to acknowledge the loss,{{refn|group="n"|According to Warner's timekeeper, the fourth quarter ran for 49 minutes and according to official statistics, there were 52 plays in the first half and 52 plays in the fourth quarter.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=50}}}} Warner's 29-game winning streak came to an end. [[Moon Ducote]] kicked the 41-yard, game-winning field goal for the Naval Reserve, and Warner called him "the greatest football player I ever saw".{{cite news|title=Richard Ducote Dies In Orleans |url=https://www.dropbox.com/sh/fspuovnvqdnd5bu/AACDhN1-amnaoGtWVhgk9-J3a?dl=0&preview=Ducote%2C+Richard+OBIT+State+Times+Adv+BR+26-Mar-1937.tiff |date=March 26, 1937|work=State Times}} Despite the loss, a number of selectors named the 4–1 1918 Panthers national champion.{{cite web | url=http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/national_championships/yearly_results.php?year=1918 | title=Yearly National Championship Selections: 1918 National Champions | access-date=April 8, 2009 | website=cfbdatawarehouse.com | archive-date=February 11, 2010 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100211113033/http://cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/national_championships/yearly_results.php?year=1918 | url-status=dead }} The team was led by freshman running back [[Tom Davies (American football)|Tom Davies]], who averaged 150 yards per game over his four-year career. The [[1919 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1919 season]] began with high expectations; World War I was over, and key players had returned from service.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=43}} However, things did not go Warner's way; at the beginning of the season, problems with the offensive line and on the flanks became apparent. Their first defeat was at [[Syracuse University|Syracuse]], where the [[Syracuse Orange football|Orangemen]] won 20–3. The 1919 Panthers had six wins, two losses and one tie.{{cite web |title=1919 Pittsburgh Panthers Stats |website=Sports-Reference |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/pittsburgh/1919.html |access-date=February 8, 2016 |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160322021022/http://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/pittsburgh/1919.html|archive-date=March 22, 2016}} They were undefeated in [[1920 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1920]], with ties against [[Syracuse Orange football|Syracuse]] and undefeated [[1920 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|Penn State]]. In [[1921 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1921]] the team's record dipped to 5–3–1, but Pitt made college football history on October 8, 1921. Harold W. Arlin announced the first live radio broadcast of a college football game in the United States from Forbes Field on [[KDKA (AM)|KDKA]], as the Panthers defeated [[1921 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|West Virginia]] 21–13 in the annual [[Backyard Brawl]].{{sfn|Sciullo|1991|page=116}} Although Warner announced before the [[1922 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1922 season]] that he was leaving to take the head-coaching position at [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford]], he honored his contract and remained at Pitt through 1923. The 1922 team had an 8–2 record, and the season ended with the Panthers taking their first cross-country train trip to defeat Stanford 16–7 in [[Palo Alto]] (coached by two Pitt assistants, sent ahead by Warner). [[Andrew Kerr]] became head coach at Stanford during Warner's last two years at Pitt.{{Harvnb|Pope|p=299}} Warner's final season was his worst at Pitt, as the Panthers stumbled to a 5–4 record in [[1923 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1923]]. However, the Warner era ended on a high note with a 20–3 victory over Penn State on November 29.{{cite news|url=http://stanforddailyarchive.com/cgi-bin/stanford?a=d&d=stanford19231210-01.2.16&e=-------en-20--21--txt-txIN-student+army+training+corps------|date=December 10, 1923|title="Pop" Warner Will Winter In Florida; Here in Spring|work=The Stanford Daily|issue=48|volume=64}} === Stanford === [[File:1924Stanfordcoaches.jpg|thumb|upright=1.15|alt=Three men crouched and one standing|[[1924 Stanford football team|1924 Stanford team]]: line coach [[Claude E. Thornhill]], Warner, assistant Andrew Kerr and team captain [[Jim Lawson (American football)|Jim Lawson]].]] Football on the [[West Coast of the United States|Pacific Coast]] had been on the rise since the late 1910s.{{refn|group="n"|At the [[1917 Rose Bowl]], the [[Oregon Ducks football|University of Oregon]] defeated [[1916 Penn Quakers football team|University of Pennsylvania]] 14 to 0. While at the [[1920 Rose Bowl]], Oregon lost to one of the recognized national champions, [[1919 Harvard Crimson football team|Harvard]], by one point: 6 to 7. [[1921 Rose Bowl|The next year]], [[Andy Smith (American football)|Andy Smith]]'s [[1920 California Golden Bears football team|University of California team]] beat an undefeated [[1920 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]] 28 to 0, making California the widely agreed national champions of the 1920 season.{{cite web|title=1920 National Championships|url=http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/national_championships/yearly_results.php?year=1920 |website=cfbdatawarehouse.com|access-date=February 9, 2016 |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160331142938/http://cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/national_championships/yearly_results.php?year=1920 |archive-date=March 31, 2016 }}}} Early in 1922, Warner signed a contract with Stanford University in which he would begin coaching in 1924 (after his contract with Pitt expired).{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=48}} Health concerns, a significant pay raise and the rising status of Pacific Coast football made Warner make the big change. Years later, he wrote:
I felt my health would be better on the Pacific coast. Weather conditions at Pittsburgh during the football season are rather disagreeable, and much of the late season work had to be done upon a field which was ankle deep in mud. At the close of every season I would be in poor physical condition, twice being rendered incapable of coaching while I recuperated in a hospital. Doctors advised me that the climate of the Pacific coast would be much better for a man of my age and in the work in which I was engaged.{{Harvnb|Miller|page=135}}
In [[1924 Stanford football team|1924]], Warner began his nine-year tenure at [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford University]].{{refn|group="n"|Stanford was founded in 1887 and had [[Stanford Cardinal football|fielded a football team]] every year since [[1892 Stanford football team|1892]], with the exception of [[1906–17 Stanford rugby teams|1906 to 1918]], when football was dropped due concerns over the sport's increasing numbers of injuries and deaths. Along with other west coast schools the sport of rugby was played instead.{{Cite journal|title=From Football to Rugby—and Back, 1906–1919: The University of California-Stanford University Response to the "Football Crisis of 1905"|url=http://library.la84.org/SportsLibrary/JSH/JSH1984/JSH1103/jsh1103b.pdf|journal=Journal of Sport History|volume= 11| issue = 3 (Winter, 1984)|pages=23 and 28}}}} When he began coaching, Stanford was one of nine teams in the [[Pacific Coast Conference]] (PCC). Warner inherited a notable squad from the previous year, including [[Ernie Nevers]] (whom Warner considered his greatest player) and All-American ends [[Ted Shipkey]] and [[Jim Lawson (American football)|Jim Lawson]].{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=55}} A season highlight was the final game against Stanford's [[Big Game (American football)|arch-rival]] [[1924 California Golden Bears football team|California]] at [[California Memorial Stadium]], the last game of the regular season. Before the game, both teams were undefeated and Stanford had not beaten California since 1905.{{refn|group="n"|In [[1906–17 Stanford rugby teams|1906]], concerned with the growing levels of violence in football, both schools stopped playing American football and switched to rugby as their university's main sport. California switched back to football in 1915, with Stanford waiting until 1919.}}{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=55}} Nevers did not play due to a broken ankle.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=57}} Late in the game, California was leading 20–3; California coach [[Andy Smith (American football)|Andy Smith]], sure the game was over, began substituting regular players.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=50}} Warner seized the opportunity to combine passing with the [[trick play]]s for which he was known (a fake reverse and a full [[spinner play|spinner]]), and Stanford made a comeback. The game ended in a 20–20 tie.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=50}} [[File:Ernie Nevers.jpg|thumb|upright=0.80|Ernie Nevers, whom Warner called his greatest player.]] Because the game was California's second tie, Stanford was chosen to play in the [[1925 Rose Bowl|Rose Bowl]] on New Year's Day against the [[University of Notre Dame]]'s [[1924 Notre Dame Fighting Irish football team|Fighting Irish]] coached by [[Knute Rockne]]. Like Warner, Rockne is considered one of the greatest coaches in football history. According to journalist [[Allison Danzig]], "With the exception of Knute Rockne of [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame]], Pop Warner was the most publicized coach in football."{{Harvnb|Danzig|page=221}} The game was thus a test of two different and highly influential systems of football: "the Warner system with the [[Wingback (American football)|wing backs]], unbalanced line and gigantic power [and the] [[Notre Dame Box|Knute Rockne system]] with its rhythmic, dancing [[Shift (gridiron football)|shift]], lightning speed, balanced line and finely timed blocking".{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=58, 59}}cf. {{Harvnb|Nelson|page=156}} Notre Dame's [[offensive backfield|backfield]] was composed of the renowned [[Four Horsemen (American football)|Four Horsemen]]. Nevers played all 60 minutes of the game, and rushed for 114 yards, more yardage than the Four Horsemen combined.{{cite web|title=Bowl Game Recaps|page=129 |url=http://grfx.cstv.com/photos/schools/nd/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/1924--75/box_score/stats_20121210aaa.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160409023618/http://grfx.cstv.com/photos/schools/nd/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/1924--75/box_score/stats_20121210aaa.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 9, 2016|access-date=September 24, 2016}} Warner's offense moved the ball but was unable to score, and Notre Dame won 27–10.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=61}} During the [[1925 Stanford football team|1925 season]], Stanford lost just one PCC game (to Washington);{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=62}} California was finally defeated, 27–7. It was the first year of a new rivalry, with coach [[Howard Jones (American football coach)|Howard Jones]] and the [[USC Trojans football|University of Southern California]] (USC) team.{{refn|group="n"|Jones won [[1921 Iowa Hawkeyes football team|1921]] and [[1922 Iowa Hawkeyes football team|1922]] [[Big Ten Conference|Big Ten conference]] titles while heading the [[Iowa Hawkeyes football|University of Iowa]].{{cite web|url=http://www.iowalum.com/magazine/football_history/1921.html|title=Gridiron Glory 100+ Years of Iowa Football 1921|website=www.iowalum.com|archive-date=June 26, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160626215407/http://www.iowalum.com/magazine/football_history/1921.html}}{{cite web |url=http://www.iowalum.com/magazine/football_history/1922.html|title=Gridiron Glory 100+ Years of Iowa Football 1922|website=www.iowalum.com|archive-date=June 26, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160626215403/http://www.iowalum.com/magazine/football_history/1922.html}}}} In their first game, at the [[Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum|Los Angeles Memorial Colosseum]], Stanford scored twice in the first half but had to hold off the charging Trojans in a 13–9 win. Because of the loss to Washington, Warner's team was not invited to the Rose Bowl.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=62}} Stanford won all its [[1926 Stanford football team|1926]] games, crushing California 41–7 and narrowly defeating [[1926 USC Trojans football team|USC]] 13–12.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=63}} Warner's team was invited to the [[1927 Rose Bowl|Rose Bowl]] to play [[1926 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|Alabama]]. Like the game against the Fighting Irish, Stanford dominated but the result was a 7–7 tie.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=63}} After the game, both teams were recognized as national champions by a number of publications.{{cite web|url=http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/national_championships/nchamps_year.php|title=Recognized National Championships by Year|website=www.cfbdatawarehouse.com|access-date=October 28, 2016|archive-date=October 15, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161015173918/http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/national_championships/nchamps_year.php|url-status=dead}}{{refn|group="n"|[[Parke H. Davis]] selected the [[1926 Lafayette Leopards football team|Lafayette Leopards]], coached by [[Herb McCracken]], Warner's former player at Pittsburgh, as national champion.{{Harvnb|National Collegiate Athletic Association|2015|page=108}}}} The [[1927 Stanford football team|1927 season]] was one of underachievement and ultimate success. Stanford lost its third game to non-conference [[1927 Saint Mary's Gaels football team|St. Mary's College]].{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=65}} Stanford's next loss was against non-conference [[Santa Clara Broncos football|Santa Clara]]. The game against USC was a 13–13 tie.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=65}} However, that year, Stanford defeated California 13–6. The game included a [[bootleg play]], the invention of which some credit to Warner. Powers stated that,
Stanford put the game on ice in the fourth period when Pop introduced the bootlegger play, which was to be widely copied and still is in use. On the original bootlegger, Warner made use of [[Biff Hoffman]]'s tremendous hands. Hoffman would take the pass from center and then fake to another back. Keeping the ball, he would hide it behind him and run as though he had given it to a teammate. Sometimes defensive players would step out of Hoffman's path, thinking he was going to block. Hoffman "bootlegged" for the touchdown against California ...{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=66}}
Despite the two losses, Stanford finished the season as PCC co-champion. They were invited to the [[1928 Rose Bowl]] against Pitt, Warner's former team now coached by protégé [[Jock Sutherland]]. Warner broke his losing Rose Bowl streak, defeating Sutherland 7–6.{{cite web|url=http://www.rosebowlhistory.org/rose-bowl-1928.php|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070718120918/http://www.rosebowlhistory.org/rose-bowl-1928.php|url-status=usurped |archive-date=July 18, 2007|title=Rose Bowl 1928|access-date=October 3, 2016|website=rosebowlhistory.org}} The win was Warner's last appearance at the Rose Bowl.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=67}} In recognition of his Rose Bowl accomplishments, Warner was inducted into the Rose Bowl Hall of Fame in 2018.{{Cite web|title=George Halas, Randall McDaniel, Pop Warner and Vince Young to be Inducted into the Rose Bowl Hall of Fame Class of 2018 |url=https://rosebowlgame.com/news/2018/9/10/general-george-halas-randall-mcdaniel-pop-warner-and-vince-young-to-be-inducted-into-the-rose-bowl-hall-of-fame-class-of-2018.aspx|access-date=2021-12-14|website=Tournament of Roses - Rose Bowl Game|date=September 10, 2018 }} The [[1929 Stanford football team|1929 season]] is known for Warner's regular use of the [[hook and lateral]], a play that involves a receiver who runs a [[Curl (route)|curl pattern]], catches a short pass and immediately laterals the ball to another receiver running a [[crossing route]].{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=68}} According to the October 25, 1929 ''[[The Stanford Daily|Stanford Daily]]'', "The trickiness that Pop Warner made famous in his spin plays and passing is very evident ... The [[Freshman|frosh]] have been drilling all week on fast, deceptive forward and lateral pass plays, and together with the reverses will have a widely varied attack".{{cite web|work = The Stanford Daily |date=October 25, 1929|url = http://stanforddailyarchive.com/cgi-bin/stanford?a=d&d=stanford19291025-01.1.3&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-------|access-date = February 11, 2016|title=Bruin Frosh Invade Farm Tomorrow |volume=76|issue=19}} That season brought Warner his second straight loss to Jones, with Stanford defeated by the Trojans 7–0. USC won the conference, and went to the [[1930 Rose Bowl|Rose Bowl]].{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=68}} Jones went on to win every year thereafter, including [[1932 Stanford Indians football team|1932]], Warner's last season at Stanford. Because of the five consecutive defeats, Warner was severely criticized by Stanford alumni.{{refn|group="n"|During Warner's latter years at Stanford, USC became the undisputed leader of the west, winning multiple national championships.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=70, 71}}}} In all, Warner and Jones played eight games; Jones won five, Warner two and one was a tie.{{Harvnb|Pope|page=300}} Against Stanford's main rival, California, Warner won five games, tied three and lost one.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=70, 71}} ===Temple=== Warner left Stanford for [[Temple University]] in [[Philadelphia]], his final head-coaching job, after the 1932 season.{{refn|group="n"| Stanford replaced Warner with [[Tiny Thornhill|Claude "Tiny" Thornhill]], his assistant coach and also one of his star players at Pittsburgh, for the [[1933 Stanford Indians football team|1933 season]]. That season Stanford beat [[1933 USC Trojans football team|USC]] 13–7, ending the Trojans' 23-game unbeaten streak. Stanford won the PCC and played in the [[1934 Rose Bowl|Rose Bowl]], but lost there to Columbia 7–0.{{cite web|url=http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/active/s/stanford/1930-1934_yearly_results.php|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150421095614/http://cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/active/s/stanford/1930-1934_yearly_results.php|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 21, 2015|title=Stanford Game by Game Results|website=cfbdatawarehouse.com|access-date=September 24, 2016}}}} He was paid $75,000 for five years (equivalent to ${{Inflation|US|.075|1933|r=1}} million in {{Inflation-year|US}}){{Inflation-fn|US}}, one of the largest salaries ever offered a coach at the time.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=72}} The [[1934 Temple Owls football team|1934 team]] was undefeated during the regular season, losing to [[1934 Tulane Green Wave football team|Tulane]] in the [[1935 Sugar Bowl|first Sugar Bowl]]. A star of the game was [[David Smukler|Dave Smukler]], whom Warner considered one of his great fullbacks.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=72}} In later years Warner said he regretted his decision to leave Stanford for Temple.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=70, 71}} He left because of concern about the school's changing funding priorities. The university leadership was planning to make Stanford primarily a graduate school; because of an increase in the number of [[Junior college#United States|junior colleges]] in California, the administration saw less need for undergraduate instruction at Stanford.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=70, 71}} Because fewer students were admitted, higher grade requirements for incoming students made admission more difficult and student athletes began enrolling at USC and California instead of Stanford. Warner soon realized that he had made the wrong decision; due to the economic effects of the [[Great Depression]], the number of applicants to Stanford decreased significantly and athletes were again admitted.{{sfn|Powers|1969|pp=70, 71}} Temple upset the [[1938 Florida Gators football team|Florida Gators]], coached by future Temple coach [[Josh Cody]], 20–12 in Warner's last game.{{cite web | url=http://www.foxsports.com/college-football/story/temple-37-vanderbilt-7-owls-seven-turnovers-game-delayed-lightning-first-win-over-sec-1938-082914 | title=Worth the Wait: Temple stuns Vandy; first win over SEC foe since 1938 | website=foxsports.com | date=August 29, 2014 | access-date=October 7, 2016}} ===San Jose State=== While coaching at Temple, Warner continued living in Palo Alto (where Stanford is located). After his 1938 retirement he was immediately recruited as an advisor to [[Dudley DeGroot]], a former center at Stanford and now the head coach at [[San Jose State University|San Jose State College]] (near Palo Alto).{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=72}} Officially an advisor, Warner was immediately put in charge of the offense. According to Powers, "DeGroot had been using a single back offense but Pop immediately changed to the double wing, much to the doubts of San Jose players. However, the formation began to click and San Jose not only enjoyed an undefeated season but was the highest scoring team in the nation."{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=73}} That year the [[San Jose State Spartans football|San Jose State Spartans]] played against [[College of the Pacific (University of the Pacific)|College of the Pacific]], coached by [[Amos Alonzo Stagg]]. It was the first time the two coaches had met since 1907, when Warner was coaching Carlisle and defeated Stagg's University of Chicago 18–4.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=73}} Warner and DeGroot's San Jose State defeated Stagg's [[Pacific Tigers football|Pacific Tigers]], 39–0.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=73}} ==Personal life and death== Warner married the former Tibb Lorraine Smith in Springville on June 1, 1899.{{Harvnb|Miller|page=47}} He smoked Turkish Trophy [[cigarette]]s and drank so much [[Alcoholic drink|alcohol]]; his trainers were instructed to supply him with "cough medicine". Warner enjoyed painting in watercolors{{cite web|url=http://www.askart.com/artist/Glenn_S_Warner/11008667/Glenn_S_Warner.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150911234712/http://www.askart.com/artist/Glenn_S_Warner/11008667/Glenn_S_Warner.aspx |archive-date=September 11, 2015 |title=Glenn Warner - Artist, Fine Art Prices, Auction Records for Glenn Warner |date=September 11, 2015 |access-date=October 31, 2016 |url-status=dead }}{{cite web|url=http://ethomashallstudio.com/art.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161021231803/http://ethomashallstudio.com/art.html |archive-date=October 21, 2016 |title=Art, Luigi Sciocchetti, Gustave Wiegand, Blue mountain Lake, Pop Warner, Lyman Byxbe, Jerry Fresia, Glenn S. Pop Warner, Lyman Byxbe, Mary V. Wheelhouse |date=October 21, 2016 |access-date=October 31, 2016 |url-status=dead }} and used the funds from his paintings to pay for his law school education at [[Cornell Law School|Cornell]].{{cite news|url=http://stanforddailyarchive.com/cgi-bin/stanford?a=d&d=stanford19311109-01.2.55#|title=Art Gallery Has Gridiron Coaches' Painting Exhibits|date=November 9, 1931|work=The Stanford Daily|issue=28|volume=80|page=4|author=Harry McMasters}} He also had a [[woodworking]] shop in his garage. Warner retired from San Jose State (and coaching) in 1940. Warner died on September 7, 1954, at age 83 in Palo Alto from [[Head and neck cancer|throat cancer]].{{cite news |agency=[[Associated Press]] |title=Mrs. Glenn Warner Dies |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=9E06E2DD1E3DE733A25756C0A9679D946091D6CF |quote=Mrs. Tibb Loraie Warner, widow of Glenn (Pop) Warner, died yesterday at her home. Her age was 90.|newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 5, 1961 |access-date=February 6, 2015 |url-access=subscription }} ==Coaching legacy== For his contributions to football, the [[American Football Coaches Association]] (AFCA) gave Warner its [[Amos Alonzo Stagg Award]] in 1948.{{Harvnb|Menke|page=129}} His name is widely known for the [[Pop Warner Little Scholars]] program, which began in 1929 as the Junior Football Conference in Philadelphia to keep children busy and out of trouble. In 1934, soon after Warner joined Temple, he agreed to the program's renaming as the Pop Warner Conference, which still endures.{{cite web|title=History of Pop Warner |url=http://www.popwarner.com/About_Us/history.htm |date=February 5, 2016 |access-date=February 23, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 5, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160205083032/http://www.popwarner.com/About_Us/history.htm}} As of 2016, about 325,000 children between the ages of 5 and 16 are mentored. ===Innovation=== [[Andrew Kerr]], who was an assistant to Warner at Pittsburgh and Stanford, said he considered Warner "the greatest creative genius in American football." [[Morris Bishop]], a Cornell professor of history, wrote that Warner "caused more rule changes than all the other coaches combined."{{Harvnb|Bishop|2014|page=345}} Warner invented the single and double wing formations,{{Harvnb|Otto|pages=139; 202–203}}Jim Campbell, [http://www.profootballresearchers.org/archives/Website_Files/Coffin_Corner/14-04-470.pdf "The Power and the Glory: Single-Wing Football"], ''The Coffin Corner'', Vol. 14, No. 4 (1992). the three-point stance,{{Harvnb|Whittingham|pages=54–55}} and the modern body block technique.{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=80}} He introduced several plays, such as the trap run,{{cite web|url={{College Football HoF/url|id=1313}}|title="Pop" Warner|publisher=National Football Foundation|access-date=September 24, 2016}} the [[bootleg play|bootleg]],{{sfn|Powers|1969|p=66}} the naked reverse,{{Harvnb|Balthasar|page=36}} and the [[screen pass]].{{Harvnb|Walsh|page=71}} He was among the first to use the [[huddle]], to [[Play calling system|number plays]], and to teach the spiral pass and spiral punt.{{Harvnb|Pope|page=292}}{{Harvnb|Warner|page=32}} He improved [[Shoulder pads (sport)|shoulder]] and thigh pads;{{Harvnb|Manchester|page=63}} and was the first to utilize adjustable fiber, rather than cotton.
